paragraphs.text: At this point you may perhaps reply that the things I mentioned, which have not been done although they could have been done, are divine works; but that for a human being to be without sin belongs to that human being’s own work, and that this work is the best, the one by which righteousness becomes full and perfect and complete in absolutely every respect; and that for this reason it must not be believed that no one has been, or is, or will be in this life who has accomplished this work, if a human being can accomplish it. But you must consider that, although it belongs to the human being to do this, this too is a divine gift, and so you must not doubt that it is a divine work. For it is God who works in you, says the Apostle, both to will and to work, for the sake of good will.

flags.quoteSource: Deus est enim qui operatur in vobis, ait Apostolus, et velle et operari, pro bona voluntate
flags.quoteTarget: For it is God who works in you, says the Apostle, both to will and to work, for the sake of good will
flags.note: Phil. 2:13 as Augustine quotes it (his Old Latin text: velle et operari), translated as the author’s text and not taken from an English Bible; to be replaced later with a licensed edition.

flags.quoteTarget: for the sake of good will
flags.note: The Latin leaves open whose good will is meant (God’s good pleasure, or the good will that God works in the human being). The rendering keeps the preposition and leaves the question open.

flags.quoteTarget: this too is a divine gift
flags.note: munus can be a gift or a task or duty. Gift is chosen because the argument that follows (God works both the willing and the working) makes the human task itself God’s gift; the profile also renders gratuitum munus as free gift.
opus (opera) is rendered work(s) throughout, together with operari, to work (Phil. 2:13); proposed for the glossary.

paragraphs.text: Accordingly, those who say that a human being lives here, or has lived here, without any sin at all are not very troublesome, and they must be pressed to show, if they can, that it is so. For if anyone is able to teach that the testimonies of the Scriptures, by which, I think, it has been settled that no human being living here is found without sin, even though he uses free will (such as Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no one living will be justified, and other such texts), are to be understood otherwise than they sound, and demonstrates that one person or several have lived here without any sin, then whoever does not both refrain from opposing him in the least and even congratulate him heartily is driven by no slight goads of envy. Moreover, even if no one is, or has been, or will be perfect in such purity—which I am more inclined to believe—and yet it is maintained and thought that there is, or has been, or will be such a person, the error, as far as I can judge, is neither great nor pernicious, when someone is mistaken through a kind of benevolence; provided, however, that whoever holds this view does not think that he himself is such a person unless he has truly and clearly perceived that he is.

flags.quoteSource: Ne intres in judicium cum servo tuo, quoniam non justificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens
flags.quoteTarget: Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no one living will be justified
flags.note: Ps. 142:2 (Vulgate numbering) as Augustine quotes it from the Old Latin; non ... omnis vivens is rendered no one living. Translated as the author’s text; to be replaced later with a licensed edition.

flags.quoteSource: qui non ei, non solum minime adversatus, verum etiam plurimum gratulatus fuerit
flags.quoteTarget: whoever does not both refrain from opposing him in the least and even congratulate him heartily
flags.note: The Latin is elliptical: non before ei negates the whole pair non solum ... verum etiam, so the envious person is the one who does not both refrain from opposing and heartily congratulate (the only reading that fits invidentiae stimulis). Rendered with does not both ... and even. The punctuation of the edition (ei,) may be worth checking against another edition.

paragraphs.text: But those must be resisted most sharply and most vehemently who think that the strength of the human will, by itself and without the help of God, can either perfect righteousness or make progress by holding a course toward it; and when they begin to be pressed on how they presume to assert that this happens without divine help, they hold themselves back and do not dare to utter this statement, because they see how impious and intolerable it is. But they say that these things do not happen without divine help because God both created the human being with free will and, by giving commandments, himself teaches how a human being must live; and God certainly helps in that, by teaching, he removes ignorance, so that a human being may know what he must avoid and what he must seek in his works, and so that thereby, through the free will implanted by nature, entering upon the way that has been shown and living with self-control, righteously, and piously, he may deserve to reach a life at once blessed and eternal.

flags.quoteTarget: make progress by holding a course toward it
flags.note: tenendo is read as holding a course (tenere ad, to steer toward) and proficere as advancing, the second member of vel justitiam posse perficere, vel ... proficere. Alternative reading: advancing by holding to righteousness. The wordplay perficere / proficere is only partly kept (perfect / make progress).

flags.quoteTarget: created the human being with free will
flags.note: liberum voluntatis arbitrium is rendered with the glossary term free will (liberum arbitrium); the genitive voluntatis is absorbed in the term, not omitted.

flags.quoteSource: continenter et juste et pie vivendo
flags.quoteTarget: living with self-control, righteously, and piously
flags.note: continenter is rendered with self-control (continently would be read as chastity only); juste is rendered righteously, in line with the righteousness family. Proposed for the glossary: continentia, self-control.
praeceptum is rendered commandment, to be kept apart from lex (law); proposed for the glossary.
adiutorium, ops (divina) and adiuvare are rendered help (to help); proposed for the glossary.
mereri is rendered to deserve (the opponents’ claim of merit); proposed for the glossary together with meritum, merit.

notes: No quotation marks are added round Scripture quoted by the author, because the Latin has none; the quoted spans are identified by the CITAT_BIBLIC flags. hic is rendered here (in this life). Pelagius is not named in the Latin and is not added.
